sentences.text: Mimodactylus was a pterodactyloid pterosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Lebanon.
The holotype specimen represents the first complete pterosaur discovered from the Afro-Arabian continent.
Evidence of unfused bones indicates the animal was likely a juvenile when it died.
The preserved skull measures 99 millimeters in length, while the preserved lower jaw measures 105 millimeters.
Its tail was extremely short, with only seven vertebrae visible that quickly diminished in size towards the rear.
The holotype had a wingspan of 132 centimeters, though the specimen was far from fully developed.
The snout is wide but not rounded at the front, ending in a sharp point.
It was the first istiodactyliform discovered in Gondwana, whereas other members of the group were previously known only from Early Cretaceous sites in Europe and Asia.
The only known specimen was found in a limestone quarry near Hjoula in the Sannine Formation.
The specimen was collected from a private quarry near Hjoula, Lebanon, over fifteen years before it was scientifically described in 2019.

The species Mimodactylus libanensis was named and described in 2019 by Alexander Wilhelm Armin Kellner, Michael Wayne Caldwell, Borja Holgado, Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia, Roy Nohra, Juliana Manso Sayão, and Philip John Currie.
Researchers suggested in 2019 that Mimodactylus likely had unique feeding habits distinct from other pterosaurs.
Mimodactylus possessed a broad rostrum and widely spaced, robust, pointed teeth adapted for seizing shrimp in the water.

Researchers noted that while insectivory could not be ruled out, Mimodactylus's broad rostrum was consistent with a primarily crustacean diet, similar to extant ducks, boat-billed herons, and shoebills.
Its short, straight, non-serrated conical teeth would have been useful for breaking the exoskeletons of arthropods.
This could indicate it was an insectivore, but insects are absent from the Lagerstätte layers.
Its elongated wings did not provide the maneuverability needed to catch fast-flying insects, but would allow stable flight during dynamic flight over the sea surface.
Mimodactylus likely had limited maneuverability during flight but was highly stable, similar to albatrosses and other open-sea fliers.
Researchers suggest that dynamic soaring, flying with little flapping, may have been the mode of flight for large pterosaurs including Mimodactylus.

The site is rich in crustacean fossils belonging to the order Decapoda; such shrimp-like creatures could have been scooped from the water surface by the wide beak, similar to how some ducks, herons, and bitterns capture prey.
The genus Mimodactylus was established by Kellner et al. in 2019.
The parent group of Mimodactylus is the family Mimodactylidae.
Kellner and colleagues named the clade containing Mimodactylus and Haopterus Mimodactylidae within the group Lanceodontia.
In 2019, Mimodactylus was placed within the clade Lanceodontia and the Istiodactyliformes.
The pteroid bone points clearly towards the neck and articulates with the proximal syncarpus; this had been a point of discussion among researchers.
Mimodactylus lived in present-day Lebanon during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 95 million years ago.
Mimodactylus lived about 95 million years ago during the late Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous.
Mimodactylus lived during the Cenomanian stage, between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
When Mimodactylus was described, insects had not been discovered at Hjoula and terrestrial plant fossils were very rare there.
It is debated whether Mimodactylus was insectivorous, as insectivorous pterosaurs like anurognathids typically have slim, well-spaced, isodont teeth.
A 2021 study by Jiang Shunxing and colleagues placed Mimodactylus in an unresolved polytomy with Haopterus, Yixianopterus, and Linlongopterus.
In 2022, Yizhi Xu and colleagues classified Mimodactylus as the sister taxon of Linlongopterus, with Haopterus at the base of their clade.
